title: Freizeit & Hobbys (Free Time & Hobbies)
description: Talk about what you do in your free time — hobbies and activities, your first regular verb endings, arranging to meet a friend, describing your day, and saying when your birthday is.

notes.heading: 📌 Hobbies & Activities (Hobbys und Aktivitäten)
notes.body:
To say what you like doing, you need hobby words and the verbs that go with them.

| German | English |
|---|---|
| Fußball spielen | to play football |
| Tennis spielen | to play tennis |
| Klavier spielen | to play the piano |
| lesen | to read |
| schwimmen | to swim |
| Musik hören | to listen to music |
| fernsehen | to watch TV |
| Rad fahren | to ride a bike |
| zeichnen | to draw |
| kochen | to cook |
| Freunde treffen | to meet friends |
| Computerspiele spielen | to play computer games |

Notice: **spielen** works for sports AND instruments (Tennis spielen, Klavier spielen). Many hobby words are international words — das Hobby, das Tennis, der Computer — so they are easy to remember.

notes.heading: 🔑 Regular Verbs: ich / du / er-sie-es
notes.body:
Most German verbs are regular: take the **stem** (infinitive minus -en) and add the ending.

**spielen (to play):**
- ich spiel**e** — I play
- du spiel**st** — you play
- er/sie/es spiel**t** — he/she/it plays

**machen (to do/make):** ich mache, du machst, er macht

**hören (to hear):** ich höre, du hörst, sie hört

The same endings (-e, -st, -t) work for hundreds of verbs: wohnen, kochen, lernen, zeichnen.

Useful sentences:
- Ich spiele gern Fußball. — I like playing football. (**gern** = with pleasure; not gern = do not like)
- Spielst du Tennis? — Do you play tennis?
- Sie hört gern Musik. — She likes listening to music.

In a yes/no question the verb comes **first**: Spielst du gern?

notes.heading: 🔑 Arranging to Meet (Wann? Wo?)
notes.body:
Useful question words for making plans:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| Wann? | When? |
| Wo? | Where? |
| Um wie viel Uhr? | At what time? |
| Was machst du? | What are you doing? |

A typical mini-dialogue:
— Hallo, Tim! Hast du Lust, ins Kino zu gehen?
— Ja, gern! Wann?
— Am Samstag. Um wie viel Uhr?
— Um drei Uhr?
— Okay. Wo treffen wir uns?
— Vor dem Kino. Bis dann!

Useful phrases:
- Hast du Lust...? — Do you fancy...?
- Wollen wir...? — Shall we...?
- Gehen wir schwimmen! — Let's go swimming!
- Das passt (mir nicht). — That suits me / does not suit me.
- Vor dem Kino / vor der Schule — in front of the cinema / the school

notes.heading: 📌 Mein Tag (My Day)
notes.body:
To describe your day, learn the parts of the day and typical activities:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| am Morgen | in the morning |
| am Vormittag | late morning |
| am Mittag | at midday |
| am Nachmittag | in the afternoon |
| am Abend | in the evening |
| in der Nacht | at night |
| aufstehen | to get up |
| frühstücken | to have breakfast |
| zur Schule gehen | to go to school |
| Hausaufgaben machen | to do homework |
| ins Bett gehen | to go to bed |

Example paragraph:
*Am Morgen stehe ich um sieben Uhr auf. Ich frühstücke und gehe zur Schule. Am Nachmittag mache ich meine Hausaufgaben und spiele Fußball. Am Abend sehe ich fern. In der Nacht schlafe ich.*

Telling the time: **Es ist drei Uhr.** (It is three o'clock.) **halb vier** = half past three (literally half to four!).

notes.heading: 📌 Dates & Birthdays (der Geburtstag)
notes.body:
The months (die Monate):

| German | English |
|---|---|
| Januar | January |
| Februar | February |
| März | March |
| April | April |
| Mai | May |
| Juni | June |
| Juli | July |
| August | August |
| September | September |
| Oktober | October |
| November | November |
| Dezember | December |

Asking about birthdays:
- Wann hast du Geburtstag? — When is your birthday?
- Ich habe am 3. Mai Geburtstag. — My birthday is on 3 May.

German dates use **am + ordinal + month**: am ersten Mai (on 1 May), am zweiten Juni (on 2 June), am zwölften Dezember (on 12 December). The ordinals 1–19 end in **-ten** (zweiten, zehnten), from 20 they end in **-sten** (zwanzigsten).

Useful: die Party (party), das Geschenk (present), der Kuchen (cake), die Kerzen (candles).

notes.heading: ⚠️ Word Order with Time Expressions
notes.body:
The golden rule of German sentences: **the verb is always the second idea** (V2).

- Ich spiele am Samstag Fußball. — I play football on Saturday.
- Am Samstag spiele ich Fußball. — On Saturday I play football.

Both are correct! When a time expression like *am Samstag* or *heute* comes first, the subject (ich) moves **after** the verb. The verb never moves from position two.

⚠️ **Common mistake:** *Am Samstag ich spiele Fußball.* — This is wrong: the verb must come second, right after the time expression.

Another rule: time usually comes **before** place.
- Ich spiele **am Samstag** **im Park** Fußball. — time first, then place.

Common time expressions: heute (today), morgen (tomorrow), am Montag (on Monday), am Wochenende (at the weekend), jeden Tag (every day).

notes.heading: ✅ Likes & Dislikes (gern / nicht gern / lieber)
notes.body:
To give your opinion about activities, put the little word **gern** after the verb:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| Ich spiele gern Tennis. | I like playing tennis. |
| Ich spiele nicht gern Tennis. | I do not like playing tennis. |
| Ich schwimme lieber. | I prefer swimming. |
| Ich koche am liebsten. | I like cooking best of all. |

The ladder: **gern** (like) → **lieber** (prefer) → **am liebsten** (like best).

Other opinion phrases:
- Das macht Spaß! — That is fun!
- Das ist langweilig. — That is boring.
- Das ist toll / super! — That is great!

✅ **Check:** translate — I like swimming, but I prefer reading. → *Ich schwimme gern, aber ich lese lieber.*

⚠️ **Common mistake:** do not say *ich mag schwimmen* with a verb — **mögen** takes a noun (Ich mag Pizza), while verbs take **gern** (Ich schwimme gern).

flashcards.example: Ich spiele gern Fußball. — I like playing football.
Am Abend lese ich ein Buch. — In the evening I read a book.
Im Sommer schwimme ich jeden Tag. — In summer I swim every day.
Sie hört gern Musik. — She likes listening to music.

flashcards.term: ich spiele / du spielst / er spielt
flashcards.definition: I play / you play / he plays (regular verb endings -e, -st, -t)
flashcards.example: Spielst du Tennis? — Do you play tennis?

flashcards.definition: gladly; added after a verb to mean 'like doing' something
flashcards.example: Ich koche gern. — I like cooking.
Wann treffen wir uns? — When shall we meet?

flashcards.definition: on Saturday (am + day of the week)
flashcards.example: Am Samstag spiele ich Fußball. — On Saturday I play football.
Wann hast du Geburtstag? — When is your birthday?
Ich habe am zwanzigsten Juni Geburtstag. — My birthday is on 20 June.
Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf. — I get up at seven o'clock.

flashcards.definition: best of all (gern → lieber → am liebsten)
flashcards.example: Ich sehe am liebsten fern. — I like watching TV best of all.

questions.explanation: Schwimmen means to swim. To read is lesen, to sing is singen and to sleep is schlafen — all similar-looking verbs, so learn them carefully.
Hören means to hear or listen, so Musik hören is to listen to music. To play music (an instrument) would be Musik machen or an instrument spielen.

questions.stem: What is someone asking when they say Wann hast du Geburtstag?
questions.explanation: Wann means when, and der Geburtstag is the birthday, so the question asks when your birthday is. How old you are would be Wie alt bist du?

questions.stem: Which word means to get up?
questions.explanation: Aufstehen means to get up. Fernsehen is to watch TV, frühstücken is to have breakfast and zeichnen is to draw.

questions.stem: What does gern add to a sentence like Ich schwimme gern?
questions.explanation: Gern after a verb means you like doing that activity: Ich schwimme gern = I like swimming. The negative is nicht gern.

questions.stem: How do you say I like playing football in German?
questions.explanation: Gern comes straight after the conjugated verb: Ich spiele gern Fußball. Nicht gern would mean you do NOT like it, and the verb must stay in second position.

questions.stem: Which is the correct du-form of spielen?
questions.explanation: Regular verbs take -st with du: du spielst. The -e ending goes with ich, -t with er/sie/es, and spielen is the infinitive.

questions.stem: How do you ask At what time? in German?
questions.explanation: Um wie viel Uhr? is the fixed phrase for asking at what time something happens: Um wie viel Uhr treffen wir uns? — At what time shall we meet?

questions.stem: What does Ich habe am zwölften Dezember Geburtstag mean?
questions.explanation: Zwölften comes from zwölf (12) with the ordinal ending -ten, so the birthday is on 12 December. German dates use am + ordinal + month.

questions.stem: Put it in order: On Saturday I play tennis. Which German sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: When a time expression starts the sentence, the verb stays in second position and the subject follows it: Am Samstag spiele ich. The verb never leaves position two.

questions.stem: A friend says Hast du Lust, ins Kino zu gehen? What are they asking?
choices: If you have been to the cinema
If you fancy going to the cinema
If you know the way to the cinema
questions.explanation: Hast du Lust...? means Do you fancy...? — it is a friendly way to invite someone to do something, here going to the cinema (ins Kino).

questions.stem: Which sentence has correct German word order?
questions.explanation: With heute (today) in first position, the verb machen must come second, then the subject: Heute mache ich meine Hausaufgaben. German is a verb-second language.

questions.stem: Es ist halb vier — what time is it?
questions.explanation: German halb vier literally means half to four, so it is 3:30 — the half hour counts towards the NEXT hour, unlike English half past.

questions.stem: What is the difference between Ich schwimme gern and Ich schwimme am liebsten?
choices: The first means you like swimming, the second that you like it best of all
The first is past tense, the second is future
They mean exactly the same thing
The first is negative, the second is positive
questions.explanation: Gern means you like doing something; am liebsten is the superlative — you like it best of all. The full ladder is gern → lieber → am liebsten.
With er (he), regular verbs take the ending -t: er hört. The -e form is for ich, -st for du, and hören is the infinitive which cannot follow er.
